# Gajakumbhajātaka (Ja 345)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
According to its commentary, the tale is introduced with the verse opening *Vanaṁ yadaggi dahatīti* and was delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana concerning a slothful monk of gentle birth from Sāvatthi who, after taking ordination, fell victim to indolence and neglected proper reflection and monastic duties [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883].
In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was a wise minister (*paṇḍitāmacco*) serving a king who was excessively sluggish [Ānandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. The Bodhisatta pointed to a slow-moving creature (*gajakumbha*, glossed as a tortoise) to illustrate its lethargic traits; hearing the Bodhisatta's counsel, the king reformed his conduct and became industrious (*analaso*) [Ānandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1883]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the tortoise with the lazy monk and himself as the wise minister [Fausböll 1883]. The Jātaka was also commemorated in the Old Burmese/Mon epigraphic captions of temple paintings at Pagan, where the Bodhisatta is explicitly recorded as the minister (*amāt*) [Luce et al. 1970].
No cross-language matches in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan collections are recorded for this text on DharmaNexus [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali tradition, DharmaNexus identifies seven passages of text reuse between the canonical verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (vol. 3), including a major correspondence between segments §2.1–4.4 and commentary section §1138_0–1145 [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
